t: as it is said: “and had I eaten a sin offering today, would it have been good in the eyes of the Lord?”. These are Aaron's words to Moses on the day his two sons, Nadav and Avihu, died: he could not eat the sin offering although eating offerings is a positive commandment, because his sons died that day. From here it is learned that the mitzvah of mourning applies on the first day alone. But the mitzvah of mourning itself is learned from the verse “for her he may defile himself” (Leviticus 21:3), which requires the kohen to become impure for his relatives when they die, and therefore also to mourn for them (Kinat Soferim on Sefer ha-Mitzvot positive commandment 37; Lechem Mishneh; and see below 2:6; and see Radbaz, who explained differently).

which is the day of death and the day of burial. But if the burial is on a different day, there is no mourning by Torah law, neither on the day of death nor on the day of burial (Aruch ha-Shulchan 399:1, but see Lechem Mishneh).
although it is said in the Torah. When Joseph and his brothers took our father Jacob to his burial.
the Torah was given and the halachah was renewed. And we do not determine halachah from what was practiced before the giving of the Torah.
and the seven days of feasting. After the wedding (see Hilchot Ishut 10:12).
the golel. The cover of the grave.
the things that a mourner is forbidden. Detailed below 5:1.
when the child died. The first son born to him from Bathsheba, who was decreed to die (see II Samuel 12:14-20).
those executed by the government, whom they do not allow to be buried. Who were killed by the authorities, who do not allow their bodies to be returned for burial.
even if they have not despaired of stealing them. Since theft is not common, mourning should not be delayed for this.
once they have despaired of searching. When they have given up the search for his body, they begin counting seven and thirty days.
they do not count for him. They do not begin counting seven and thirty days.
to another country. To another city.

and anyone who did not live thirty days etc.. When it is not known for certain whether nine months of pregnancy were completed and he did not live thirty full days, we are in doubt whether he is defined as a viable child or a stillborn, and we are lenient not to mourn for him (Kesef Mishneh).
even if he died on the day he was born, they mourn for him. Because he stayed in his mother's womb a full nine months, he is considered viable even if he died the same day.
a nine-month child. Who stayed nine months in his mother's womb.

and an eight-month child. Who is known for certain to have been born after eight months in his mother's womb, and therefore is considered a stillborn even if he lived more than thirty days (see Hilchot Shabbat 25:6).
cut up. Whose limbs were severed in his mother's womb and emerged in order, for example the hand emerged and then the leg, and so on.
scrambled. Whose limbs were severed in his mother's womb and emerged out of order (see Rambam's Commentary on the Mishnah, Niddah 3:5).

and they do not occupy themselves with them. With eulogy, funeral procession and the like; but in caring for the body and the needs of the bier and burial they do occupy themselves for them (Tur Yoreh De'ah 344, and similarly wrote Responsa of the Rashba 1:563). It is possible to explain that they do not even occupy themselves in caring for the body and its bier as is done for other dead, but only bury (see below, halachah 11, 4:1, Hilchot Yom Tov 1:23).
all those executed by the government. For example, one who rebels against the king or insults him (see Hilchot Melachim 3:8).
and they do not withhold from them anything. Of the things done for the honor of the dead.
and their property goes to the king. See also there 4:9.

but for all those executed by the court, they do not mourn... until the flesh decays. Because those executed for sin by the court do not have their sins atoned for at the time of death but only when the flesh decays, so at the beginning of mourning, which is the sealing of the grave, they are not fit for mourning, and therefore their mourning was postponed entirely (Rambam's Commentary on the Mishnah, Sanhedrin 6:8; and see also Hilchot Sanhedrin 13:6).
but onenim, for aninut is only in the heart. They are permitted to grieve for them, since heartache is not defined as an act of mourning.
the minim. The heretics (see Hilchot Teshuvah 3:7-8; the "min" mentioned here is a general term for all the types of heretics mentioned there).

and the meshumadim. Those who transgress deliberately and in rebellion against the commandments of God, even one who transgresses a single sin in order to spite (Hilchot Teshuvah there 3:9, Hilchot Rotzei'ach 4:10).
and the informers. Those who hand over their fellows or their property to gentiles or violent people (Hilchot Teshuvah 3:12).
stand over him in a row. After the burial of the dead, the comforters stand in rows on leaving the cemetery and pass the mourners one by one and comfort them (see below 13:1-2).
the blessing of mourners. Things said in the mourner's house (below 12:7).
and anything that is an honor to the living. Things by which his relatives are honored.
not one who climbed to the roof and fell and died. Perhaps he fell by accident and did not intend to take his own life.

and they saw him go up immediately in anger or in distress. That immediately after he threatened that he intended to climb to the top of the roof in order to fall from it, they indeed saw him go up to the roof in his anger or from his distress.
but if they saw him etc.. And they had not heard from him earlier that he intended to take his own life.
his sword. His blade.
he is in the presumption of all the dead. And we do not regard him as one who took his own life.
and by their words. By the words of the Sages (see Rulings and Opinions).
his married wife. Married to him, excluding his betrothed (as below, halachah 3).
that he does not become impure for his brother and sister from his mother. As below, halachah 12.
nor for his married sister. As below, halachah 10.
his son or brother who came from a maidservant or from a gentile woman. Who was born to a Canaanite maidservant or to a gentile woman and follows his mother, and is a slave or a gentile.
and likewise one who converted, he and his sons, or was freed, he and his mother. After converting or being freed he is considered like a newborn and is not related to his parents or brothers.

and not an onen. An onen is a person whose close relative for whom he is obligated to mourn has died; on the day of death he is an onen by Torah law, and on the night after the day of death he is an onen by rabbinic law. An onen is forbidden to offer sacrifices and to eat sacrificial food and second tithe (see Hilchot Ma'aser Sheni 3:5-7, Hilchot Bi'at Mikdash 2:9-10). [Note: in the words of the halachic authorities the term "onen" refers to a person whose dead lies before him and has not yet been brought to burial; the laws of this situation are explained in the Rambam below 4:6 and in Rulings and Opinions there.]
he mourns with them. When a relative dies for whom they are obligated to mourn.
in their presence. When he is with them.
his son's brother. A brother of his son by another mother.
his son's mother. After he divorced her.
he overturns his bed. He turns over his bed (as below 5:18).
or her son. By another man.

and likewise anything similar. When the relationship of the deceased to his relatives is not one of blood kinship but a relationship through marriage, he is not obligated to mourn with his relatives for them.
in what cases does this apply. That it is a mitzvah to become impure, and that they make him impure against his will.
since they are not warned about impurity. As below 3:11.
by rabbinic law. By the words of the Sages.

they made her like a met mitzvah etc.. Although the prohibition of a kohen's impurity is from the Torah and mourning for his wife is only rabbinic, since they equated her to a met mitzvah, the prohibition of a kohen's impurity is set aside for her burial (Radbaz; for the law of a met mitzvah see below 3:8).
all those for whom we said they do not mourn. Above 1:9-11.
until the grave is sealed. Until they cover the grave.
the disqualified. Challalim, born of a divorcee who married a kohen.
mamzerim. Born of forbidden sexual relations (except one born of a niddah; see Hilchot Issurei Biah 15:1).
his disqualified wife. Who is forbidden to him and whom he must divorce.
one who heard that her husband died and married etc.. The law is that she is forbidden to both husbands and needs a get from both (see Hilchot Gerushin 10:5).

a challalah. A woman who was forbidden to the priesthood and had relations with a kohen, or a woman born of a kohen's marriage to a woman forbidden to him (Hilchot Issurei Biah 19:1). This applies only if she was disqualified after he was born; but if she was disqualified before he was born, this son is a challal and is not warned against becoming impure for the dead (as below 3:11).

even though she is married to a kohen. Although she retained the sanctity of the priesthood regarding eating terumah and the like, he does not become impure for her (Tiferet le-Moshe Yoreh De'ah 373).
a bogeret. A girl who reached age twelve and a half, whose signs of virginity have diminished and who is no longer called a complete virgin (see Bavli Yevamot 60a-b, Hilchot Issurei Biah 17:13).
struck by a stick. Whose virginity was lost as a result of injury, not from intercourse.
one whose existence was by the hand of a man. Who had relations with a man.
who has not been to a man, except a betrothed woman. Who was betrothed to another and had not yet had relations.
also his brother and sister who are fit to inherit him. Only his brother and sister from his father are fit to inherit him (see Hilchot Nachalot 1:7).
the offspring that were mixed up. And it is not known for certain who the father of each child is.

and the son who is doubtfully a seven-month child of the later one or a nine-month child of the first. A woman who was divorced or widowed and did not wait three months before remarrying, and a son was born to her, and there is doubt whether he was born at seven months to the last husband or at nine months to the first husband.

and likewise any woman divorced with a doubtful divorce. Where there is doubt whether the divorce took effect, for example he threw her a get in the public domain and it fell midway between them (Hilchot Gerushin 5:12).
or with an invalid get. A get invalid by rabbinic law (see there 10:2), while by Torah law the woman is divorced.

for a limb from the living of his father. If a limb was cut from his father before he died, the kohen does not become impure for the burial of this limb (see below 3:1 for the explanation that a kohen is forbidden to become impure for a limb from the living).
nor for a bone of his father's bones. If a bone or limb is missing from his father after he died, he does not become impure for burying this bone.
and likewise one who gathers his father's bones. Who collects them from their first burial place to bring them for burial elsewhere.

even though the spine exists. The spinal column exists. And although a complete spine makes one who touches it impure like a whole corpse (see Hilchot Tumat Met 2:8), for the purpose of permitting a kohen's impurity it is not considered a whole body.

impurity for relatives is pushed aside and not permitted for all. The kohen's prohibition of impurity is set aside for the mitzvah of mourning for relatives, but this does not permit him to become impure for other people.
except for the six dead who are specified in the Torah. His mother and father, his son and daughter, his brother and his virgin sister (Leviticus 21:1-3).
or his wife. Whose impurity is rabbinic (above 2:7).
one who touches the dead. Who touched a corpse with his body (Hilchot Tumat Met 1:3).
one who overshadows. Who overshadowed the dead with his body, or the dead overshadowed him, or who stayed with the dead under one tent (there 1:10).
one who carries. Even though he does not touch the dead or the impurity itself with his body; likewise one who moves the dead or the impurity is considered a carrier and becomes impure (there 1:6-7).

or the other impurities that separate from the dead. For example a limb and flesh that separate from the dead. Likewise a limb cut from a living person makes impure like a corpse by Torah law and a kohen is forbidden to become impure for it (see there 2:1-4, and see above 2:14).
for it is said: “for a person he shall not defile himself”. All impurities separating from the dead whose prohibition is from the Torah are included in “person” (Radbaz).
and we already explained in Hilchot Tumat Met. Chapters 2-3.

all the things that make impure from the dead, by the Torah or by their words. If he became impure through things whose impurity is from the Torah, he receives lashes by Torah law; and for things whose impurity is rabbinic, he is given disciplinary lashes by rabbinic law (below, halachah 13).

if the kohen touched a grave, he receives lashes. Even though he did not touch the dead himself. Likewise if he overshadowed the grave or stayed with the grave under one tent, he receives lashes, since a grave makes impure even through a tent (Hilchot Tumat Met 2:15).

but he may touch garments that touched the dead. Garments that touched the dead make impure one who touches them with seven-day impurity, but this impurity is not from the Torah (see there 5:3-5). And although the kohen is warned also about rabbinic impurities (as below, halachah 13), he is permitted to become impure by this one even initially.
and likewise if he entered an impure tent into which the impurity entered. He entered a place that is impure because impurity in an adjacent room entered it through one of its doors or windows.

and we already explained all the tents into which impurity enters or from which it leaves. The places that are impure because the impurity enters them, and the places from which the impurity inside spreads to another place.
and the law of the projections and the protrusions. Tree branches that shade the ground and stones protruding from a wall that shade the ground (see Hilchot Tumat Met 13:2).
and all that bring the impurity. Under which the impurity spreads.
and those that interpose before the impurity. Things through which the impurity does not penetrate.
all of it in Hilchot Tumat Met. Mainly in chapters 12-19.
and there we explained. Hilchot Tumat Met 1:13.
that gentiles do not make impure by tent. For it is said regarding the war against Midian: “anyone who touches a slain person” (Numbers 31:19), and no tent is mentioned there.
and therefore their graves are pure. For the impurity of a grave is by the law of tent.

the time of a prostration, as we explained regarding the impurity of the Temple. For a person who entered the Temple pure and became impure must leave immediately, and if he stayed there for the length of time of a prostration lying on the ground (which is the time it takes to say the verse in II Chronicles 7:3: “and they bowed with their faces to the ground on the pavement and prostrated and gave thanks to the Lord, for He is good, for His kindness is forever”), he is liable (Hilchot Bi'at Mikdash 3:21-23).
and separated. He let go of his contact with the dead.
he receives lashes for each and every one. Although he has not yet been purified from his earlier impurity, he receives lashes for becoming impure through a new act of impurity.
and returned and touched, and they had warned him. Before he touched.

for he is defiled and remains so as long as he has not separated. Since he did not separate from the impurity, there is no new act of impurity, and therefore he does not receive lashes (compare Hilchot Nezirut 5:16-17).

and the one who made him impure transgresses “and before the blind you shall not place a stumbling block”. For anyone who strengthens the hands of transgressors or causes them to stumble transgresses this prohibition (Hilchot Rotzei'ach 12:14). But one does not receive lashes for this prohibition because it is a prohibition that includes many matters (a "general prohibition" - see Sefer ha-Mitzvot rule 9, Hilchot Sanhedrin 18:3).
if the kohen was unwitting and the one who made him impure was deliberate, the one who made him impure receives lashes. See also Hilchot Kilayim 10:31, Hilchot Nezirut 5:20.

from this you learn that he is liable for “he shall not enter” and liable for “he shall not defile himself”. Unlike an ordinary kohen, who in cases where he is forbidden to become impure and became impure transgresses only “he shall not defile himself”; a high priest transgresses also “he shall not enter.”
he entered the tent and sat there until the dead person died on him etc.. Compare Hilchot Nezirut 5:18.

or entered a shidah, teivah or migdal. Vessels which, if their volume is greater than forty se'ah, do not receive impurity (see Hilchot Kelim 3:2). And when their cover is closed, one inside them does not become impure (see Hilchot Tumat Met 21:1).
and his fellow came and removed the roof of the shidah over him. His fellow opened the cover of the vessel (compare Hilchot Nezirut there).

for impurity and entry come as one. In these two cases the impurity and the staying in the tent of the dead came at once, and therefore he receives lashes for both. But if the kohen entered in the ordinary way a tent that had a dead person in it, he receives one set of lashes, because entry and impurity do not come together, as from the moment he put in his nose or feet he was already impure, so his impurity preceded his entry (see there).
he became impure earlier etc.. For example, he touched the dead and became impure, and after he separated from the first impurity he entered a tent, and after he entered a person died there.
from the mouth of the tradition. The tradition of the Sages.
a kohen and a nazir were walking on the road etc.. Compare Hilchot Nezirut 7:13.

for his sanctity is not an eternal sanctity. For unlike the priesthood, which is an intrinsic sanctity that applies to the kohen from birth, the sanctity of a nazir, even a lifelong nazir, stems from his acceptance of nezirut, and he also has the possibility of annulling it.
and the segan. The one appointed as deputy to the high priest (Hilchot Kelei ha-Mikdash 4:16).
the anointed for war. The one appointed to address the people at the time of war, anointed for this role with anointing oil (Hilchot Melachim 7:1).

let the anointed for war become impure and let the segan not become impure. Although the anointed for war ranks above the segan (see Hilchot Kelei ha-Mikdash 4:19), regarding impurity the segan has priority, since one of his duties is to replace the high priest in the Yom Kippur service if he becomes impure (Bavli Nazir 47b).
the nasi. The head of the Sanhedrin or the king (Yad Peshutah, and see Hilchot Sanhedrin 26:1).

and likewise everyone is an onen for him. They are forbidden to eat sacrificial food and second tithe and cannot offer sacrifices, as with an onen (Yad Peshutah; for the explanation of the term onen in the Rambam's words see above 2:2 in the commentary).
the challalim. One born of a kohen's marriage to a woman forbidden to the priesthood (Hilchot Issurei Biah 19:5-6), and also one whose father is a challal (there halachah 14).
the court is not commanded to separate him, but his father must educate him in holiness. See also Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 17:27-28.

a dead person occupies four cubits of his own for impurity. Out of concern that one might not know where the dead lies and might overshadow it, the Sages decreed impurity on an area of four cubits around the dead.
a rebellion lashing. Lashes by rabbinic law.

to a beit ha-peras. A field in which there was a grave and which was plowed, so that now bones of the dead are scattered throughout the field, and the Sages decreed corpse impurity upon it (see Hilchot Tumat Met 10:1).

to outside the Land. The Sages decreed corpse impurity on the soil of the lands of the gentiles because they are not careful to bury in one place and it is likely that the soil contains the bone of a dead person the size of a barley grain (there 2:16, Rambam's Commentary on the Mishnah, Oholot 2:3).

by blood of tevusah. A revi'it of blood in which blood that left the dead person while alive is mixed with blood that left him after death; this blood makes impure by rabbinic law (Hilchot Tumat Met 2:13).

by the golel and the dofek. The golel is the cover placed over the grave, and the dofek are the stones that support the golel from the sides; they make impure by tent and by touch by rabbinic law (there halachah 15).
as we explained in Hilchot Tumat Met. 2:13-16, 5:11.

but if he entered a cemetery, he receives lashes by Torah law. For on entering the cemetery he overshadows the graves, and a grave makes impure by tent by Torah law (there 2:15). But if he does not overshadow the graves and is within four cubits of the graves, he is given disciplinary lashes (as explained at the beginning of the halachah), and outside four cubits it is permitted (Radbaz).

a kohen is permitted to become impure in a beit ha-peras or outside the Land for a matter of a mitzvah etc.. Since this is rabbinic impurity, the prohibition is set aside for the mitzvah of procreation or Torah study.
and likewise he may become impure by rabbinic impurity for the honor of people. For human dignity overrides a rabbinic prohibition (see also Hilchot Kilayim 10:29).

and likewise they step over coffins of the dead. Wooden coffins in which the dead are placed: if there is an open space of a handbreadth between the dead and the coffin lid, it is considered a tent that interposes against impurity, and when there is no open space of a handbreadth the coffin does not interpose and the impurity bursts through and rises. And although most coffins have an open space of a handbreadth, the Sages decreed impurity on all coffins because of the minority that have no such space (see Hilchot Tumat Met 12:6).
to meet kings. Out of respect for royalty.
even kings of the nations, in order to distinguish etc.. So that when Israel's honor is restored, he will be able to see the greatness of the reward of the kings of Israel.
because he saves from their hand. He saves his property from them.
they close. They shut the eyes.
and they plug his orifices. They stop up the orifices of the body so that wind does not enter them (Hilchot Shabbat 26:20).
and anoint him with kinds of spices. To remove a bad smell from him.
and they cut his hair. If it was too long.
in a cloth. A scarf, a garment.

so as not to shame the poor whose faces are blackened by hunger. At first they would uncover the faces of the rich and cover the faces of the poor because they turn black from hunger, and the living poor were ashamed that they were buried differently, so they enacted that the dead person's face always be covered (see Bavli Mo'ed Katan 27a).
and they carry. They bear.
it will snap. It will tear.
and he turns out to be delayed from the mitzvah. He will stop to fix his sandal and not be able to continue carrying the bier.
a koch. A grave.
and they return the earth and stones on top. They cover the dead or his coffin with earth.
and they may. They are permitted to.
and they mark the graves. They mark the burial place with lime so that kohanim can avoid grave impurity (Rambam's Commentary on the Mishnah, Ma'aser Sheni 5:1).
and they build a nefesh on the grave. A monument.

and a person shall not turn to visit the graves. Some explain that this refers to a prohibition of opening the grave (Radbaz; and see Responsa Chatam Sofer part 2, Yoreh De'ah 336). Others explain that this is the conclusion of the previous sentence, that one should not visit the graves of the righteous because their deeds are their memorial, and a person should turn and look to the memory of their good deeds (Kesef Mishneh based on Responsa Rivash 421). Others explain that it refers to a prohibition of turning to attain a spirit of impurity or communicate with the dead by visiting cemeteries (Yad Peshutah, and see Hilchot Avodah Zarah 11:13).
the goses. One in his last breaths (Rambam's Commentary on the Mishnah, Arachin 1:3).
and cool vessels. Cold vessels.
to a dripping candle. Whose burning may continue for some time.
and they do not place him on sand or on salt. They used to lay the dead on cool sand or salt so that he would not decay quickly from the heat of the cushions and pillows he lay on.
the one who closes. Who closes the eyes of the dead immediately when he dies.
and they do not bare the shoulder. Which is one of the mourning customs (below 8:3).
and they do not bring a coffin and shrouds into the house until he dies. So that the goses's mind not be unsettled, and so that they do not despair of praying for him (Yad Peshutah).
one whose dead lies before him. Who has not yet been buried.
eats in his fellow's house. And does not eat in front of the dead.
makes a partition. Between himself and the dead.
turns his face. Turns his body to the other side.
and either way. Even if the dead does not lie directly before him, and this dead person is his relative whom he is obligated to bury.

he does not recline and eat. He should not eat reclining, which is a manner of permanence and there is concern he may forget the needs of the dead (Shitah Mekubetzet Berakhot 17b); some explained that one may not recline because reclining is a manner of distinction (Rashi there).
and does not eat meat and does not drink wine. So that he not be drawn after them and become lax about the needs of burial (Tosafot and Ran Mo'ed Katan 23b).
and does not bless. The blessing of ha-motzi before the meal.
and does not invite. The Grace after Meals after the meal (Rashi Berakhot there).
and they do not bless for him. He does not need others to bless on his behalf to fulfill his obligation.
and they do not invite for him. He does not join the zimun (there).

and is exempt from reciting the Shema etc.. Out of respect for the dead and because he is preoccupied with the mitzvah of burying him (Meiri there 18a; and see also Hilchot Kriyat Shema 4:3, which explains that one who digs the grave and one who guards the dead are also exempt).
and from all the commandments. Positive commandments, but he is forbidden to do prohibitions.
except for marital relations. That he is not obligated to fulfill the mitzvah of onah, but if he wishes he may (Lechem Mishneh, Yad Peshutah).
not to become satiated. He should not drink a great deal, which could lead to drunkenness and distract him from the mourning (see also below 13:8).

they hasten his bier immediately. They hurry to bring his bier to burial, so as not to burden the public too much (Rabbeinu Yitzchak Gei'at, Hilchot Evel p. 232, and for other reasons see Beit Yosef).
and for his father and mother it is disgraceful. For out of respect for them he should prolong their eulogy and funeral.
it was the eve of Shabbat or the eve of a festival. And there is no time to delay and prolong the eulogy and funeral.
rains are pouring. Falling.
permitted. To hurry the burial of his father and mother.
one who leaves his dead overnight. Leaves him without burial.

transgresses a negative commandment. For it is said regarding those executed by the court: “you shall not leave his body overnight on the tree, but you shall surely bury him that day” (Deuteronomy 21:23), and the Sages learned that the law is not only for those executed by the court, but for all the dead (Hilchot Sanhedrin 15:7-8, and see there and below 12:1 that there is also a positive commandment to bury the dead on the day of death).
and he is obligated to sit on an overturned bed. An upside-down bed (and see also below 5:18).
a mat. A rush mat.

for it is said in Ezekiel... implying that all the people are forbidden. When God informed Ezekiel that his wife would be taken by a plague, He commanded him not to follow the customs of mourning, and from there the Sages learned what the mourning customs are that a mourner generally must observe.
your glory. "Glory" is a term for tefillin (see Bavli Berakhot 11a).

implying that all the people eat from others' food on the first day and are forbidden to eat from their own. Thereby the mourner will not occupy himself with preparing food and be distracted from the mourning, and since others are commanded to feed him, they will naturally look after his needs, support him and comfort him.
on the first day by Torah law. For the mourning customs on the day of death and burial are from the Torah (as above 1:1).
to have a haircut. To get a haircut.
and to set the bed upright. Rather he must overturn all the beds in the mourner's house (as below, halachah 18).
and to let his head go bare. Rather he must cover his head (as below, halachah 19).

for He warned the sons of Aaron: “do not let your heads go bare”. After the death of Nadav and Avihu, God warned their brothers Elazar and Itamar not to behave by growing their hair, and from this the Sages learned that a mourner grows his hair and does not cut it.
and any hair he has. Even hair in covered places.
both the one who shaves and the one who is shaved. He is forbidden to remove his hair, whether himself or by others.
mustache. Moustache.

for it is said: “please mourn” etc.. Joab son of Zeruiah commands the wise woman to pretend to be a mourning woman, and the verse concludes: “and be like a woman who has been mourning for the dead for many days” (II Samuel 14:2).
and put on mourning garments. From here it is learned that a mourner must wear unlaundered garments.

and washing is included in anointing, since washing precedes anointing. Although the verse speaks only of anointing, since anointing is the last stage of washing, it is understood that washing is also forbidden.
garments. Clothes.

new and pressed white ones. But colored garments, even if new and pressed, a mourner is permitted to wear, because their newness and pressing do not significantly affect their appearance (see Meiri Mo'ed Katan 23a). Likewise new white garments that are not pressed, or old white garments even if pressed, a mourner is permitted to wear.

and pressed. Garments that were smoothed and straightened of wrinkles (Aruch, entry "gahatz"; Radbaz). Some explain that it refers to a stronger cleaning process than laundering, such as in hot water or with strong cleansers (Nimukei Yosef Mo'ed Katan 14b, and see Meiri there 23a).
and if it is to remove filth it is permitted. For they forbade only anointing for pleasure.
but in cold water he washes his face, hands and feet. For this is not washing for pleasure.
for it is said: “and David comforted Bathsheba” etc.. After the death of their child, at the end of the seven days of mourning (see Meiri Mo'ed Katan 15a).
and it is permitted to be alone with his wife though he is forbidden marital relations. And we do not suspect that he will have relations with her.
for it is said in Ezekiel etc.. See above 4:9 in the commentary.
if he was coming on the road, he wears shoes and goes. So that his feet are not injured (see also Hilchot Ta'aniyot 3:4).
and when he enters the city. When he enters the town.
and to go from town to town for trade. To travel from city to city for his business.
all the first three days. Which are the strongest part of mourning (Yerushalmi Mo'ed Katan 3:5).
and the woman spins with a spindle inside her house. A poor woman is permitted to spin with a spindle in her house (Ritva Mo'ed Katan 21b).

the things permitted to do on chol ha-moed. Work is forbidden on chol ha-moed. But work that, if not done, would cause a great loss, he is permitted to do, provided it does not involve great effort (see Hilchot Yom Tov 7:2-3).
his olives to turn. Before extracting the oil, the olives are placed in a pile to soften them, and they must be turned from time to time so they do not spoil from the heat generated in the pile.
and his jars to seal. For the opening of the barrels must be sealed after the wine or oil is put into them.
and his flax to take out of the soaking. For the raw flax placed in soaking water to soften it must be taken out so it does not rot in it.
and his wool from the pot. For the wool placed in a boiling pot for dyeing must be taken out, for if it stays there a long time it will spoil.
and they water lightly. They water with slight irrigation.

once the season of water arrives. For before sowing they water the field a little, and if they do not water it in this season and the rainy days come, the field will not be properly sown this year (Ramban Torat ha-Adam, the matter of mourning).
the sharecroppers. A sharecropper receives the field from its owner for a percentage of the crop.
and the lessees. A lessee receives the field from its owner for a fixed amount of produce.
and the contractors. The contractor mentioned here is one who pays fixed rent for the field in money (Meiri Mo'ed Katan 11b, and see Ritva, who explained differently).
these may work as they usually do. Because their work in the field is for themselves and they lose if they do not engage in it, they may work in it even when its owner becomes a mourner.

but the donkey drivers and camel drivers with his animals... these may not work. When they were not hired for a fixed time, it is a day-to-day hire, and although they work for themselves, since they can hire from someone else without loss they may not work with the mourner's animals or ship.

and if they were leased or hired earlier for a fixed time, these may work. For in a hire for a fixed time, the lessees will lose if they hire from another, and because they work for themselves, it is permitted (see Meiri there, and see the Rishonim there who explained this law in other ways).
a day laborer. One who works for the mourner in his field and receives a daily wage.
even in another city he may not do work for him. For work in the field is well known, and it is evident that he is working for the mourner (Radbaz, based on what is implied from below, halachah 13).
whether by contract. That he receives a lump-sum payment for the work.
or not by contract. That he receives a daily wage for his work.
he may not do. For a mourner is forbidden to work, and must postpone the work until after his days of mourning.
in another's house they may do. Since it is something detached from the ground and the work is done discreetly, there is no concern that this work will be attributed to the mourner.
a lawsuit with another person. A monetary claim against another person.
but if it was a matter that would be lost. For example, the defendant is about to sail to another country, or the plaintiff's witnesses are ill and may die.
Moan in silence. The Sages derived from this verse that a mourner must be silent, refraining from Torah study and from greeting others (as below 5:20).
and in aggadot. Aggadic teachings.
and if the many need him. For example, if there is no one else to teach them Torah or to rule on halakhic questions for them.
provided that he does not appoint an interpreter. That he does not appoint someone to relay his words to the public, as is customary during a sermon.
but he whispers to another at his side etc.. This change makes it recognizable that he is a mourner.
and from where do we know that a mourner does not sit on the bed. The upright bed, in its usual manner, but rather on an overturned bed.

and he lay on the ground. The Sages explained that he does not sit on the actual ground, but on an overturned bed close to the ground (see Babylonian Talmud, Moed Katan 21a; and see above 4:9, that sitting on an overturned bed is obligatory only on the first day, and on the other days he may sit on the ground).
to overturn the bed. To flip the bed, with its legs pointing up and its upper side facing down.
even ten beds in ten houses etc.. For the obligation to overturn the bed does not apply only in the house where the deceased died, but in all the houses under the mourners' control.
a bed designated for vessels or for money need not be overturned. For only a bed designated for sleeping or sitting needs to be overturned.
a dargash. A small bed.

a mourner loosens its straps and it falls by itself. The kravitim are the loops by which the leather webbing is held and tied to the frame of the bed; by loosening the loops the leather webbing drops down.

a bed whose posts protrude from it, since it is impossible to overturn it. It has two posts at the sides of the bed for spreading a sheet over it, and it is not possible to stand the bed upside down on these posts.
he sets it upright, and that suffices. He leaves it upright, and need not overturn it.

but he sleeps on an overturned bed. Throughout the seven days of mourning, in addition to the obligation to sit on an overturned bed on the first day of mourning (as above 4:9, Mirkevet HaMishneh, Yad Peshuta). Some explain that the obligation to sleep so is also only on the first day (Radbaz).
with the head uncovered. With the head bare, not covered.
you shall not cover your upper lip. That he not wrap his head up to his mustache, as mourners do.
from which it follows that the other mourners are obligated to wrap the head. See above 4:9 in the commentary.
and the headcloth with which he covers his head. With which he is accustomed to cover his head all year round.
as it says, 'and he shall cover his upper lip'. Regarding the conduct of the leper, who behaves in the manner of mourners.
like a mourner. Like a person in mourning.
all of the first three days. Which are the peak of mourning (as above 5:8).
one who greeted him. For example, one who did not know that he was a mourner.
by rabbinic enactment. By the words of the Sages.
for it says. In the passage of the beautiful woman taken captive after the war.
and in a feast of companions. A meal customary among friends (as below, halakhot 6 and 7).
and to travel on business from town to town. To go from city to city for his trade.

he must let his hair grow until it becomes unkempt. He lets his hair grow long; when his hair has grown excessively long, he is permitted to cut it after thirty days even without his friends rebuking him.
or until his friends rebuke him. Even if his hair has not grown excessively long.
garments. Clothes.

and linen garments are not subject to pressing. They are not forbidden for pressing, since pressing does not help them for long and they quickly return to being wrinkled (and according to the opinion that pressing is extra laundering - see above 5:3 in the commentary - in linen garments the pressing is not noticeable on the garment because of the coarseness of the linen cloth).

and it is permitted to betroth, even on the day of death. It is permitted to betroth the woman, lest another get ahead of him and betroth this woman. After the thirty days he marries her and brings her into his home.
if he has already fulfilled the commandment to be fruitful and multiply. That he already has a son and a daughter (Hilchot Ishut 15:4).
and he has someone to serve him. Someone who will do for him the tasks that a wife does for her husband.
and he has no young children. Who need a mother to raise them.
the three festivals. Passover, Shavuot and Sukkot.
to betroth and to marry immediately. To betroth a woman and bring her into his home, even on the day of death.

but it is forbidden for him to be with her until thirty days. Although the prohibition of marital relations applies only during the seven days of mourning, relations with a new wife involve exceptional joy.

and similarly, a woman who was in mourning may not have relations until thirty days. The commentators found this halakhah difficult, since a woman may not remarry for ninety days after being widowed, so that it can be distinguished whether she is pregnant by her first husband (see Hilchot Gerushin 11:20). Therefore some explained that it refers to a woman mourning other relatives, and although the prohibition of marital relations applies only during the seven days, relations of marriage, which involve exceptional joy, are forbidden for all thirty days (Lechem Mishneh; Bach, Yoreh De'ah 392; and the Kesef Mishneh explained that this refers to an additional prohibition on account of mourning, apart from the general prohibition for the sake of distinguishing).

a feast of companions that he was obligated to repay. Friends eat at one another's homes, and he had already been invited to his friend's before he became a mourner, and now he must repay his friend and invite him.
but if he is not obligated to repay it. He has not yet eaten at his friend's home, and now he is inviting him.
either way he may not enter a feast of companions. Even if he is obligated to repay it.

he may go on business after thirty days. Although a mourner is permitted to do business and trade after the seven days (as above 5:7), going to a distant place in a caravan involves great publicity and joy, and therefore it is permitted only after thirty days (Radbaz, Kesef Mishneh).
until his friends rebuke him. After thirty days.
if he wishes, he reduces his business etc.. After the seven days, since he is permitted to do business and trade that is not in a caravan and the like.
for his father or mother he reduces his business. After the seven days, for thirty days (Kesef Mishneh).
one who goes from place to place. This refers to a mourner for a father or mother, who must reduce his business for thirty days (as above, just before; Kesef Mishneh).
and if not. That he cannot reduce it, for example because there is no one to buy for him, and he must buy in that city because he will not have the opportunity afterward.
he buys what is needed for the road and things that involve the sustenance of life. Even though he buys himself and buys a lot.
crucified. Hanged.

it is forbidden for him to live in that city until the flesh has decayed. For when people see him they will recall his crucified relative and the dead person will be disgraced; and when the flesh has decayed his form no longer remains and he is no longer mentioned (Kesef Mishneh). Some explain that the reason is mourning: if he remains in a place where his relative is crucified, it appears he treats the mourning for him lightly, and once the flesh has decayed the obligation of mourning has already ended (Radbaz).
and if it was a large city like Antioch etc.. For in a large city people do not know one another (Kesef Mishneh).
he may. It is permitted for him.
and he goes up this way and that. For with it the laws of the seven days end and the laws of the thirty days begin.
to cut his hair. To have a haircut.
one whose mournings were piled upon him. Who had to observe two or more consecutive periods of mourning.
he lightens with a razor but not with scissors etc.. They did not permit him a full haircut, laundering and bathing, except with a modification.

and one who comes from overseas and from captivity etc.. In all these cases the person could not shave, bathe or launder his clothes, and when his mournings are piled up together with one of these cases, he may cut his hair, bathe and launder in the usual way, even without a modification.

or one who was under a ban and it was lifted. One under a ban is forbidden to cut his hair or launder until his ban is lifted (see Hilchot Talmud Torah 7:4), and his ban was lifted during the days of mourning.
or one who was bound by a vow and had the vow annulled. He vowed not to cut his hair or launder, and went to a sage who annulled the vow for him during the days of mourning.

and anyone coming out of impurity to purity. And did not cut his hair or launder his clothes during his impurity, since it is not fitting for a person in days of impurity to beautify himself (Maggid Mishneh, Hilchot Yom Tov 7:19).
if within thirty days. From the day of burial.
and he counts thirty. From the day the report arrived.
one hour. A short time.
during the festival or on the Sabbath. On these days he does not observe mourning in public (as below 10:1-3).

it counts for him. Since he cannot observe mourning on these days, they are included in the count of thirty days, and at the end of the festival or the Sabbath the report is classified as a distant report.
only one day, and part of the day is like all of it. He observes mourning for one hour.
as we have explained. Above 5:2.

if he was in a nearby place etc.. If he was within ten parsaot (about 40 km), a distance one can reach in one day of average walking (see Babylonian Talmud, Pesachim 93b), so he is considered as having been present there and it is added to the count of the days of mourning they counted.
if he found comforters at the home of the head of the household. If when he arrived they were still comforting at the home of the most important member of the family.
even though they had risen to stand. Even if the comforters had already prepared to stand and leave.
and he counts with them the completion of thirty days. He completes with them the thirty days of mourning.
from here on he goes. To another house of mourning.
the first week. The first week.
the second. The second week.
he goes out but does not sit in his place. He may leave the door of his house but does not sit in his place in the synagogue, the study hall, or any place with fixed seating.

except that he is forbidden to tear his garments at the top and to grow his hair long. These are forbidden to him by Torah law (see Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 1:10), and he fulfills the obligation of tearing by tearing his garments from below, at the bottom of the garment (Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 5:6).
and to go out after the bier. To the funeral procession; rather he remains in his house or in the Temple (ibid. 5:5).
and when they serve him the mourner's meal. For a mourner is forbidden to eat from his own on the first day, and they feed him from theirs (as above 4:9).
all the people recline on the ground. To honor him and to share in his mourning.
and he reclines on the bench. Unlike an ordinary mourner, who must sit on an overturned bed (ibid.).

and if he wished to comfort others, the appointed one places him among the people. The appointed one (also called the 'deputy') is at his right and causes the High Priest to be in the middle between him and the mourners and the people who are on the left side (as below 13:2, and see also Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash ibid. 5:4).
who does not leave the entrance of his palace. The entrance of his palace, for it is not to his honor to accompany the dead (see also Hilchot Melakhim 2:4).

and David went after Abner only to let the people know that he was not killed with his consent. Joab son of Zeruiah, commander of David's army, killed Abner son of Ner, commander of Saul's army, without David's knowledge, and David went after Abner's bier so that the people would know that he grieved over his death and that it was done against his will (see II Samuel 3:26-39).

and when they serve him the mourner's meal, all the people recline on the ground. To honor him and to share in his mourning (Yad Ramah, Sanhedrin 19a). It is possible to explain that this is the way of comforters, who sit on the ground (see below 13:3, and see also Hilchot Melakhim 2:4).
the darga. A small bed.
in front. At the front of the garment.
on the sides. At the sides of the garment.
except the High Priest, who tears from below. Out of respect for him (as above 7:6).

as it says, 'and do not tear your clothes, lest you die' - from which we learn that another is obligated to tear. When Nadab and Abihu, the sons of Aaron, died, God told their brothers Elazar and Itamar not to tear their garments, and from this the Sages inferred that another mourner is obligated to tear.

as it says, 'and the king arose and tore his garments'. This verse was said when a false report reached David that Absalom had killed all the king's sons, and from the fact that David tore while standing, the Sages learned that the obligation to tear is while standing.

and he need not separate the hem of the garment. He is not required to begin the tear exactly at the hem of the garment and separate the hem into two distinct tears, but may begin the tear below the hem and make a kind of hole in the garment, even though in this way the garment is not torn in two.
and he may tear inside. He may tear his upper garment even if it is covered by a cloak and the like.
not in front of people. He may tear even in a place where there are no people.
and he is obligated to tear only the outer garment. And not the other garments he is wearing.

and all seven days of mourning the tear is at the front. The tear must be at the front so that it is visible, except on the Sabbath, when he changes his torn garment; and if he has no other garment, he turns his garment around so that the tear is at the back (as below 10:1).
at the time of their heat. At the moment of the mourner's main distress and pain, close to the time of death.
he tears until he exposes his heart. A tear of a handbreadth is not sufficient.
and he separates the hem of the garment. He tears from the hem of the garment onward so that there are two distinct sides.
on the outside. The garment he tears must be exposed and not covered by a cloak and the like.
in front of all the people. In a place where people are present.
and he tears all the garments he is wearing. And not only the outer garment.
a sweat garment stuck to his flesh does not hinder. And he is not obligated to tear it.
and he draws his arm out of the shirt until his shoulder and arm are exposed. He takes his hand out through the tear until his shoulder and arm are exposed outside the garment.
before the bier. Before the bier on which the deceased is placed during the funeral.
a minor is torn for out of grief. So that those who see will be pained.
they do not tear for him. If he learned of the death of his relative.
and they do not inform him. If he did not learn of it.
lest his mind become unsettled. Lest his mind be disturbed by the grief.
and they silence the women before him. So that he will not know.
one who has no shirt to tear. For example, he is poor and his clothes are torn, or he has only a sweat garment, or his clothes are borrowed.
and anyone who goes out in the torn garment. Which was torn previously.
that is, that he has now torn them. As one who says that he tore it now.
and he mends. He sews up the place of the tear (although in an ordinary tear for a father or mother he is not permitted to mend at all).
and he pays him the value of his tear. For the value of the shirt was reduced by this.

he shall not touch it. For he received no permission to tear his friend's garment, unlike when he informed him before lending it, in which case the lender could have considered such a possibility and lent it with that in mind.
within the time of speaking. The time it takes to say the words 'Peace upon you, Rabbi' (Hilchot Shevuot 2:17).
he does not tear again. For within this time it is considered that he tore at the time of death.
his father died. Your father has died.
and afterward it was found to be his son. It became clear that it was his son who died and not his father.
and if after the time of speaking, he has not fulfilled his obligation. For the tear for a deceased must be specifically for that deceased (see Babylonian Talmud, Nedarim 87a).

if within the seven days he tears another tear. For if he adds to the first tear within the seven days, it will look like a continuation of the earlier tear, and it will not be recognizable that he is tearing for the additional deceased.

if it reached his navel he moves three finger-breadths away and tears. He does not tear further in the same place, but begins the new tear at a distance of three finger-breadths from the place of the earlier tear.
as will be explained. That one never mends a tear made for his father or mother (below 9:1).
for his father and mother are not part of the addition. One does not fulfill the obligation of tearing for a father or mother by an addition to another tear, out of respect for them.
he sews loosely. He sews the tear with a coarse, unstable stitch.
and mends. He sews with a precise stitch.
for his teacher who taught him Torah. His primary teacher, from whom he learned most of his wisdom (Hilchot Talmud Torah 5:9).
the Nasi. The head of the Sanhedrin.
the Av Beit Din. The deputy to the head of the Sanhedrin, who is the greatest of the seventy sages (Hilchot Sanhedrin 1:3).
blasphemy. Cursing the Name of God.
and for the cities of Judah, for Jerusalem and for the Temple. When they are in ruins (below 5:10).
and he never mends. He may not sew the tear with a straight stitch and restore the garment to its original state.
to shalal, to malal, to gather, or to make like ladders. Types of uneven sewing that do not join the garment as it was, and the tear remains noticeable.

like Alexandrian mending. Where he unravels the loose threads of the fabric and joins the tear with new weaving (it is called Alexandrian because this is how they used to mend torn garments in Alexandria).
and anyone who tears from within the shalal, malal or gathering has done nothing. For with these stitches the garment is not considered whole but as still torn.
but he may tear from within the Alexandrian mending. For this is an excellent stitch and the garment is considered whole.
even if he turned the garment over and its hem is now at the bottom. And now the tear is at the lower side of the garment.
the buyer. The purchaser.
as it says, 'and he cried out' etc.. This verse speaks of Elisha's conduct when his master Elijah the prophet ascended to heaven.
from here that he must separate the hem. To tear from the hem of the garment and separate the hem into two distinct tears (as above 8:2).
as it says, 'and David took hold' etc.. After David heard of Israel's defeat in the war against the Philistines.
as it says, 'and Eliakim came' etc.. After they heard Rabshakeh, the envoy of Sennacherib king of Assyria, blaspheming God.

and the same applies to one who hears from the mouth of one who heard. Just as Hezekiah tore when Eliakim, Shebna and Joah told him of Rabshakeh's blasphemy, as it says, 'And when King Hezekiah heard, he tore his clothes' (Isaiah 37:1; and see also Hilchot Avodah Zarah 2:10).
and witnesses are not required to tear when they testify in court. But the judges who hear the testimony do tear (Hilchot Avodah Zarah 2:8).

as it says, 'and when Jehudi read' etc.. This verse was said about the scroll that Jeremiah the prophet wrote about the future downfall of Jerusalem; when the scroll reached Jehoiakim king of Judah and was read before him, he cut it and threw it into the fire until it was burned.
forcibly and as the deed that occurred. By coercion and force, with the intent to provoke and to desecrate the Name of Heaven, like the deed of Jehoiakim.
the parchment. The parchment.
the scroll and the words. This implies that for each of them a separate tear must be made.

as it says, 'and men came... with torn clothes'. After they heard of the destruction they tore their garments (see Rashi and Radak there; and regarding these tears see also Hilchot Ta'aniyot 5:16-18).
he must tear. For it is like a Torah scroll that was burned (Babylonian Talmud, Moed Katan 25a, and see the Rishonim there).
all are obligated to tear for him. Even if they are not near him at the moment the soul departs.
and they tear a handbreadth like the other mourners. Like the tear of a mourner for other relatives (as above 8:2).
until they expose their hearts. Like the tear for a father and mother (above 8:3).
and they bare the right. They take the right arm out of the tear until the shoulder and arm are exposed (as above, there).
once they have turned their faces from behind the bier. Once they have stopped accompanying the bier on which the deceased lies and have begun to return.
for even for his teacher who died, one mourns only one day. All the more so, with a tear for a sage who is not his teacher, he may mend the tear the next day.
and they bare the left. They take the left arm out of the tear until the shoulder and arm are exposed.
and they bare both arms, from here and from there. They take out both the right and left arms from the tear, so that both shoulders and both arms are exposed.
and all the study halls are closed. And his yeshiva is not canceled for more than thirty days (as below 14:25).
and they read seven. They read from the Torah and call up seven people.
in pain. Aching, distressed.
the Sabbath counts toward the days of mourning. It is included in the count of the seven days of mourning.

such as wrapping the head. It is considered a private matter because people wrap themselves in a headcloth all year round, except that a mourner's wrapping differs slightly from ordinary wrapping in that it also covers the mouth, and this difference is not noticeable (Radbaz, and see Kesef Mishneh, who gave further explanations).
and he sets the bed upright. He returns the beds he overturned and places them as usual.
he turns the tear to the back. He turns the shirt around so that the tear is at the back.
from the afternoon onward. From the time of minchah ketanah, about two and a half hours before sunset.

it turns out that he counts after Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur twenty-three days. If he buried his dead one hour before Rosh Hashanah or before Yom Kippur, we consider that hour as seven days, and he has only twenty-three days left in which he must observe the laws of the thirty.
for the decree of the seven has been canceled. And we consider it as seven days.
Atzeret. Shavuot.

even though it is one day, it is a festival and counts as the seven days. Although the festival of Shavuot is one day, because it is a festival it is considered seven days. Together with the hour before Shavuot, which is considered seven days, he counts sixteen days after the festival.
he counts only nine days after the festival. To complete the decree of thirty.
and it turns out that the first festival day interrupts the seven. And we consider it as seven days.
and the eighth day of the festival, another festival. Because it is a festival in its own right, we consider its one day as seven days, similar to Shavuot.

for part of the day is like all of it. And with part of the seventh day the laws of the seven end (as above 6:12), and immediately afterward the thirty begin, and the decree of thirty is canceled when the festival arrives.
he does not cut his hair until he lets it grow long or until his friends rebuke him. As above 6:3.
and he is not permitted to bathe, anoint, or do anything until the festival enters. For the decree of the seven is canceled only upon the actual entry of the festival.
in all five things. Those forbidden during the thirty days (as above 6:2).

and it is permitted to cut the hair during the intermediate days, for he was compelled etc.. Although the Sages decreed that one may not cut his hair on the intermediate days of the festival, lest he not cut it before the festival and enter the festival unkempt, when it was not possible for him to cut it before the festival, he is permitted to cut it on the intermediate days (see Hilchot Yom Tov 7:17-18).
and similarly he cuts his hair after Shavuot or after Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur. When his seventh day falls on the eve of the festival.
one whose seventh day falls on the eve of the festival. And before the festival the decree of thirty is canceled for him and he is permitted to cut his hair (as above 5:5).

although it is forbidden to cut hair on the intermediate days. They permitted it only to one who could not cut his hair before the festival, but if he could and did not, it is forbidden for him to cut his hair on the intermediate days (Hilchot Yom Tov ibid. 7:19).
it is permitted to cut hair after the festival. Since the decree of thirty was canceled.

during the festival. On the intermediate days, or on the festival day by non-Jews (see Hilchot Yom Tov 1:23 and Piskei VeShitot there, and see below 10:5 for the law if they buried on the second day of the festival at the end of the festival).
he counts the seven from the last second festival day. If he was buried during the festival days.
since it is by their enactment. For it is not a Torah obligation but a rabbinic one (see Hilchot Kiddush HaChodesh 5:4-6).
it counts for him toward the count. It is included in the count of the seven days of mourning.
as we have said. Above 5:8.

on the second festival day, which is the last festival day. The second festival day of the seventh day of Passover or of Shemini Atzeret ('the second festival day of the Diaspora'); when burial takes place on this day, the care of the deceased and the burial needs are done by Jews - see Hilchot Yom Tov 1:23 and Piskei VeShitot there.
Atzeret. The festival of Shavuot.
since the second festival day is by their enactment. Its obligation is rabbinic.
and mourning on the first day is from the Torah. The obligation of mourning on the first day, which is the day of death and the day of burial, is from the Torah (as above 1:1).

for the two of them are like one long day. Unlike the other second festival days of the Diaspora, the two days of Rosh Hashanah are considered one sanctity, and therefore one does not observe mourning on the second day either, just as one does not on the first (though burial may then be done by Jews, as the law of the second festival day of the Diaspora - see Hilchot Yom Tov 1:24).
for the reason we explained in Hilchot Kiddush HaChodesh. 5:7-8.
although there is no mourning on the intermediate days. On the intermediate days of the festival (as above 10:8, and see also Hilchot Yom Tov 6:23).
and he bares his shoulder. Taking the shoulder and arm out of the garment, which is done until burial (as above 8:3).
and they serve mourners' bread on the festival. Even on the intermediate days of the festival they feed the mourner from the food of others on the first day (as above 4:9).

only relatives who are obligated in mourning. Those obligated to mourn by Torah law or rabbinic law (as above 2:1). But a tear done out of respect, for example when he tears during the mourning observed by his son or by his wife (as above 2:4-5), he does not tear on the intermediate days of the festival.
or one who tears and bares for a sage etc.. For these are obligatory tears (as above 9:11).
and everyone serves the mourners' meal for a sage on the festival. Each person feeds his friend from his own.
in the open square. In the city's open square.

for everyone is a mourner for him. Although the mourners' meal is not observed on the festival except for relatives who are obligated to mourn (see Hilchot Yom Tov 6:23), for a sage everyone must mourn, and therefore the meal is served for him.
they serve only on upright beds. Unlike an ordinary mourners' meal, where the mourner sits on an overturned bed (as above 4:9).
the blessing of mourners. Words said in the house of mourning (see below 12:7).
they stand in a row and comfort. After the burial of the deceased, the comforters stand in rows on leaving the cemetery and come to the mourners one by one and comfort them (see below 13:1-2).
and they dismiss. They dismiss the comforters to return to their homes, and they do not accompany the mourners to the house of mourning.

and they do not set the bier down in the street, so as not to encourage the eulogy etc.. They take the deceased from his home directly to burial, so that people will not come to eulogize him in the street as is done on weekdays (see also Hilchot Yom Tov 6:22-23).

he does not gather the bones of his father and mother. In the past they used to place the deceased in temporary burial and after the flesh decayed they would gather the bones and move them to a permanent burial place (see Jerusalem Talmud, Moed Katan 1:5), and this should not be done on the festival.
for he is a mourner for him. Below 12:8.
and likewise they do not eulogize the dead on Chanukah and Purim. See also Hilchot Megillah VeChanukah 2:13, 3:3.
clapping. With their hands or on their bodies as an expression of mourning.
for all of them answer together. They say the eulogy together.

a lament that one says and all answer after her. One laments aloud and the rest answer after her with what she says or with its main points, in the manner of eulogizers (Rabbenu Yonah of Gerona, Moed Katan 17a in the Rif's pages).
in his presence. When his bier lies before us.
and the day of the report of his death is like his presence. When the report of his death arrives, it is considered as if his bier lies before us, and we eulogize him.
even though it is distant. Even if the report arrived after thirty days from his death.
a woman shall not stir up grief for her dead. To stir up weeping and eulogy (and not only a woman, but any person - see Hilchot Yom Tov 6:24).
in pain. Aching, distressed.
for the dead is not forgotten from the heart for thirty days. Weeping and eulogy bring the deceased to mind, and they will enter the festival in sadness and worry.
for an old death. One who died more than thirty days before the festival.
but if he died within thirty days close to the festival, she may stir up. For in any case this deceased will not be forgotten from the heart before the festival.
the seven days of the wedding. The Sages enacted that one who marries a virgin rejoices with her for seven days (Hilchot Ishut 10:12, and see also above 1:1).
all the needs of the meal. The wedding meal.
and he slaughtered his slaughtering. He slaughtered the animals and prepared the cuts of meat.
if he had not yet put water on the meat. And the meat is still fit for sale.
they bring the deceased into a room. They delay the burial of the deceased, for if they were to bury him now, mourning would apply to the groom or the bride.

and he performs the mitzvah relations and separates. The first relations of the groom with his bride are called the mitzvah relations, and afterward he separates from her, for he must observe mourning in private matters (as explained in the next paragraph).
he observes private matters of mourning as on the Sabbath. For example, wrapping the head, the prohibition of marital relations, and bathing in hot water (as above 10:1).
and they do not prevent ornaments from the bride for all thirty days. So that she not become repulsive to her husband (compare Hilchot Shevitat Asor 3:1).
when the groom's father or the bride's mother died. For they are usually the ones who take care of preparing the meal or preparing the bride's ornaments and cosmetics.

therefore they compel the heirs etc.. Because it is the honor of the deceased, the heirs cannot evade performing the eulogy even when it involves a monetary expense, for they have no power to waive the honor of the deceased.
and if he commanded 'Do not eulogize me,' they do not eulogize him. For the deceased himself may waive his honor.
they do not listen to him. And they bury him against his wishes.

for burial is a commandment, as it says, 'you shall surely bury him'. This verse was said regarding those executed by the court, and from it they learned that there is a commandment to bury every Jew on the day of his death (Sefer HaMitzvot, positive commandment 231, and see Hilchot Sanhedrin 15:8).
they do not place a Torah scroll on the bier of a sage. Out of respect for the Torah scroll, just as it is forbidden to sit on a bed on which a Torah scroll lies (Hilchot Sefer Torah 10:6).
and they do not move him from bed to bed. For it is the sage's honor to be carried out on the bed on which he died (Babylonian Talmud, Moed Katan 25a).

not that they lower it through the roof. Even if the doorway is narrow and the bed does not pass through it, one must take care not to take the sage's bed through the roof and the like, for this is not to his honor.

and they do not make a standing and sitting for fewer than ten. Since they stand and sit seven times, it is not proper to go to such trouble when the mourners and their relatives are not ten people (Commentary on the Mishnah, Megillah 4:3). Some explained that it is not proper to speak in such an honorable style to fewer than ten people (see Babylonian Talmud, Megillah 23b).
with relatives. With the relatives of the deceased, even if they are not obligated in mourning.
on the first day. On the day of burial.
they have the other relatives and family members who are not mourners stand. Together with the mourners.
they never set a woman's bier down in the street. And not only on the intermediate days of the festival, when they do not set down a man's bier in the street either (above 11:3).

one who gathers bones. In the past they used to place the deceased in temporary burial and after the flesh decayed they would gather the bones and move them to a permanent burial place (see Jerusalem Talmud, Moed Katan 1:5).
dirges and wailing. Words of grief.
and words of rebuke. Words of moral exhortation.
his spine. The backbone.
they stand over him in a row. After the burial of the deceased, the comforters stand in rows on leaving the cemetery and come to the mourners one by one and comfort them (see below 13:1-2).
even if they moved him after twelve months. Although after twelve months mourning has ceased, since the form of his body remains, he is considered as one buried anew for these laws.
even if they are bound up for him in his sheet. Although the bones are still with him and have not yet been buried, one does not mourn more than one day.
and they do not say laments over them. Although they are his father and mother, laments are not said over them, as above 5:6.
children of the poor. For they grieve more over the loss of the child they raised in hunger and they have no other joy with which to be consoled (Rashi, Moed Katan 24b).
children of the elderly. For they do not know whether they will have more children (Ran, ibid.).
for all thirty days. Since he had not yet emerged from the status of a nefel (non-viable infant) and one can say that from the outset he was not fit to live, so the mourning for him is not so great.
carried in the arms. They carry him to burial by hand alone, not in a coffin or on a bier.
and is buried with one woman and two men. And ten men are not needed.
because of seclusion. For one man may not be secluded even with many women (see Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 22:8).
in a small coffin carried by the arms. In a small coffin carried in the arms, with no need to place it on the shoulder.
a twelve-month-old is carried out on a bier. As an adult is taken out.
they mourn. They grieve, and some explain that they cry out and weep.
one known to the public. Who is already accustomed to going out of his house and people know him.
many are occupied with him. In his funeral.
the slaves and maidservants. Canaanites who serve in a Jewish household.
they do not eulogize them etc.. Because their connection to their owners is not at all like a family connection.
may God make up for your loss. For they are bound to their owners only by a monetary tie.
and they stand beside the cemetery. In the place designated for this purpose, which is called the ma'amad (Commentary on the Mishnah, Berakhot 3:2).
and the mourners are not counted in the quorum. Since the purpose of the row is to comfort them, they are not counted.
whether new faces came. People who have not yet comforted the mourner.
or they did not come. Even people who have already comforted the mourner fulfill the commandment of comforting if they come again during the seven days of mourning.
and they sat with him on the ground. And the mourner himself sits on the ground (as above 5:17-18).
that the mourner open his mouth. In speech.
and Eliphaz answered. Only after Job began to speak did Eliphaz answer him, and not before.
and once the mourner nodded his head. As if hinting to the comforters that they should let him be.

and they sit in his place all seven days of mourning. Morning and evening, which are the times when people customarily come to comfort mourners (Radbaz); some add that they come and pray there the morning, afternoon and evening prayers (R. Yosef Kafih).
and the rest of the people gather around them. Other people come and gather around the regular ones, as is done for mourners out of respect for the deceased (Meiri, Shabbat 152a).
ten of the rest of the people gather etc.. Each day ten people who are not regulars gather there.
to stand before a Nasi. Out of respect for him.
except for a mourner and a sick person. Who are preoccupied with their mourning or illness and are not obligated to stand.
and to anyone who stands before him, a person says 'sit' etc.. Any person may tell his friend to sit, except to a mourner and a sick person, whom he does not tell to sit.
they sweep. They sweep.
and sprinkle. They sprinkle water on the dust of the floor.
and drinking vessels. Vessels for drinking.
but not the incense burner. Spices placed on coals for fragrance, for it is not proper for a mourner to take pleasure during his mourning.
the food with which they serve the mourners' meal. Above 4:9.
white. Transparent.
but a colored one. One in which what is inside cannot be seen.

one does not drink in a house of mourning etc.. The Sages enacted that those who customarily drink wine in a house of mourning drink no fewer than ten cups; later they began to add to the number of cups and people became drunk from it, and the Sages determined that one may not add to ten cups (see Babylonian Talmud, Ketubot 8b).

they do not say a tradition or aggadah in a house of mourning. Because it causes distraction from the mourning (and this prohibition applies to the comforters or relatives who are not mourners, since the mourner himself is forbidden in Torah matters, as above 5:15-16).
a tradition. Halakhic teachings.
and aggadah. Aggadic teachings.
in pain. Distressed, aching.
except matters of the dead. Torah matters related to the dead, such as the laws of funerals, burial or eulogy (see Rishonim on Berakhot 3:2).
but to engage in words of Torah. Which are not related to the dead.

in his presence or in a cemetery it is forbidden. But if he distances himself four cubits from the dead or from the grave, it is permitted (see Hilchot Keriat Shema 3:2; Hilchot Sefer Torah 10:6; and see also below 14:13).
and it is written, 'and the days of weeping and mourning for Moses were completed'. And before that it says: 'And the children of Israel wept for Moses... thirty days.'
from our holy Rabbi. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi.
when the report of his death came. The report arrived that he had died.
shake. Shake your heads in the manner of mourning and grief.
for this is the way of the world. Death is part of nature and the ordinary order of the world.
and for the other five. The five things forbidden during the thirty days (as above 6:2).
as if a sword rests on his shoulder. That he too may be killed by it, and he must conduct himself with extra awe.
placed in a corner. In a corner, where the threat is smaller but still exists.

from here on it passes opposite him in the marketplace. Although the present threat has passed, nevertheless one must always remember death and place it before one's eyes in order to learn a lesson from it (HaMaspik LeOvdei Hashem by R. Avraham ben HaRambam, cited in Yad Peshuta).
to understand his mind and return. To reflect on his ways and repent of his deeds.
and they did not tremble. They were not afraid (from the expression 'trembling and quaking').
of their words. Of rabbinic origin.
and to carry out the dead. To accompany him to burial.
and to bring in the bride. To accompany her to the wedding canopy.

which have no limit. The Sages set no maximum for a person's participation in these acts of kindness, unlike acts of kindness with one's money, for which the Sages set a measure and limit (Commentary on the Mishnah, Peah 1:1).

they are included in 'you shall love your neighbor as yourself'. They are included in this commandment, which is a positive commandment from the Torah (see Sefer HaMitzvot, second principle, and see also Hilchot De'ot 6:3, Sefer HaMitzvot positive commandment 206).
the accompanying. Accompanying guests.
as it says, 'and he saw, and behold, three men'. And Abraham our forefather ran toward them although he was receiving the Divine Presence at that time.

they compel for a funeral as they compel for charity. One who refuses to give money for a funeral, the court compels him and strikes him with disciplinary lashes until he gives the amount they assessed, similar to compulsion for charity (see Hilchot Matnot Aniyim 7:10).

even one who accompanies his friend four cubits in the city. Although his friend is not yet leaving the city, there is a commandment to accompany him four cubits. Some explain that this refers to a friend who is leaving the city; and although he does not accompany him outside the city, since he began accompanying him and continues to accompany him in thought, this helps him on the rest of his way outside the city (Maharsha, Sotah 46b).
up to the outskirts of the city. The area added to the city when the houses at a distance of about seventy cubits (about 35 meters) from the city are included (Hilchot Shabbat 28:1).

up to the Sabbath limit. Two thousand cubits around the city, which are considered the city's boundary beyond which one may not go on the Sabbath (ibid. 27:1), and the boundary is measured from the outskirts of the city outward.
a parsah. About four kilometers.
because they are occupied with the needs of the sick person. And the visitor would disturb them in their work.
he may not sit on a bed etc.. Because the Divine Presence is above the head of a sick person (see Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 12b).
nor above his head. Near his head, even if he sits at the same height, because the Divine Presence is there (see Arukh HaShulchan, Yoreh De'ah 335:7 in the name of the Zohar).
but wraps himself. He wraps himself in his tallit and sits with awe and respect.
who met. Who passed near one another.

they move the dead out of the way of the bride. They move the dead to the sides of the road and give precedence to letting the bride pass to her canopy. Since it is a matter of honor, the honor of the living comes first (Lechem Mishneh). Some explain that attending to bringing in the bride always takes precedence over attending to carrying out the dead, but the beginning of the halakhah speaks of when there are already enough people occupied with bringing in the bride and carrying out the dead, in which case it is preferable that he join those carrying out the dead (Emek She'elah 3:6).
and everyone passes aside before the king. They move to the sides of the road and let the king pass.
when he does not have all his needs. Enough people to accompany him to burial.
and everyone who is not engaged in Torah study. Everyone who is not studying Torah at that time.
is obligated to be occupied with him. Even if he has all his needs.

up to sixty myriads. Just as the Torah was given at Sinai to six hundred thousand people, so at the passing of a person who engaged in it, he is to be accompanied by six hundred thousand people (see Babylonian Talmud, Ketubot 17a).

for the sake of the ways of peace. And in Hilchot Melakhim (10:12) the Rambam connected this to the verses: 'The Lord is good to all, and His mercies are over all His works' (Psalms 145:9), 'Her ways are ways of pleasantness and all her paths are peace' (Proverbs 3:17).
and they do not read in them. One does not study Scripture in them.
and they do not study Mishnah in them. One does not study Mishnah in them.
derive benefit. Use.
and they do not behave lightheadedly in them. For example, laughter, jesting and idle talk (Hilchot Tefillah 11:6).
