and tefillin on his head. Because of the sanctity of the tefillin (see also Hilchot Tefillin 4:23).
and a Torah scroll in his arm. Even if it is wrapped in a cloth and placed in its case (see also Hilchot Sefer Torah 10:6).
and he may not pray there. And he may not recite the Shema there either (Hilchot Keriat Shema 3:2).
in a diskaya. A double sack placed on both sides of a donkey (see also Hilchot Sefer Torah 10:11).

and if it was in his field, he may remove it. If the grave to which he is carrying the dead is in the burial field of his forefathers, he may remove him there, since it is pleasant for a person to be buried with his forefathers (Jerusalem Talmud, Moed Katan 2:4, and see also Hilchot Yom Tov 8:9).
and not two dead as one. Next to each other.
and a child who goes out with his mother. A child who is attached to his mother and needs her.
the dust of the grave. The earth that is returned over the dead after he has been placed in the grave (as above 4:4).
virgin soil. The earth of the land.
one who builds a grave for a dead person, it is not forbidden until the dead is placed in it. For designating it for the dead does not prohibit it for benefit until it is actually used for the dead.
even if he placed a nefel in it, it becomes forbidden for benefit. Although one does not mourn for it or occupy oneself with it (as above 1:8).
that was made for a living person. For a person while he is alive.
and he threw. He cast, buried.
a raised portion. Something elevated (R. Yehudah Shilat; in other versions the reading is 'dimos', meaning a course, a row of stones).
everything is forbidden for benefit. Since he cannot tell where the addition forbidden for benefit is, the whole grave is forbidden for benefit.
and if he recognized the addition. If it is possible to distinguish what the addition is.
he removes it and the rest is permitted. Since it was made in advance while he was alive, it did not become forbidden when he placed the dead in it.
a nefesh. The structure built over the grave (as above 4:4; and see Commentary on the Mishnah, Oholot 7:1).

and this grave is forbidden for benefit out of respect for his father. Although with another dead person, designation does not forbid the grave for benefit until the dead is actually buried in it (as above 13:18), in this case, out of respect for his father, the grave becomes forbidden for benefit by designation alone, without his being buried in it.
except for his hair, which is permitted for benefit. See also Hilchot Sanhedrin 12:4.
and all his shrouds. All the shrouds used to wrap him and buried with him, and not only the shrouds that wrap his body directly.
garments. Clothes.
until it touches the bed that is buried with him. As below, halakhah 22.
all the garments that are thrown on the dead. Relatives, out of their grief, throw their own garments on the dead so that they will be buried with him.
lest they be confused with the shrouds. That people would think they are taking from the dead person's shrouds and using them, and would mistakenly think that the shrouds are permitted for benefit.
out of their anger. Out of anger and grief.
it is a commandment for others to save them. To take these garments before they touch the bed and become forbidden.
he transgresses 'do not destroy'. For the details of this prohibition see Hilchot Melakhim 6:10.

they hamstring a horse he rode on. They cut the horse's hooves, since this horse is considered a utensil designated for the king, and something that was designated for the king is not used by anyone else (see Hilchot Melakhim 2:1).

from the knee down. They cut its hooves from the knee down so that they cannot use it (and although this involves suffering of animals, it is set aside for the honor of a king, which is the honor of all Israel - Tosafot, Avodah Zarah 11a).
in a place that does not make it a treifah. For in a way that makes it a treifah, this would cause the animal exceptional suffering (Ritva, ibid.).

and they hold a session at his grave for seven days. His students sit and study Torah there in his honor. Although one should not engage in Torah in the presence of the dead or in a cemetery (as above 13:9), in the case of a sage who died, where many students study Torah before him, this is his honor (Responsa of R. Yosef Migash, no. 47).
and they did honor to him in his death. It is said of King Hezekiah, and the Sages expounded that they held a session at his grave.
they may burn his bed and all his utensils. Out of respect for the king, so that others will not use his utensils (see also Hilchot Melakhim 2:1).
and this does not involve the ways of the Amorites. This is not among the practices of the gentiles which it is forbidden to follow (for this prohibition see Hilchot Avodah Zarah 11:1).
as it says. To King Zedekiah.
